title: Section 208 — Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant

content.overview: Section 208 — Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant. The operative rule is the text of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. Cite the BNS section, not the repealed Indian Penal Code, for conduct governed by the BNS. Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant. Historical concordance: IPC 174. For conduct governed by the BNS, cite BNS section 208; the IPC reference is historical concordance. Punishment, ingredients and exceptions are only those the section states. Not a verified closure.

sections.body:
(a) A, being legally bound to appear before a High Court, in obedience to a subpoena issuing from that Court, intentionally omits to appear. A has committed the offence defined in this section
(b) A, being legally bound to appear before a District Judge, as a witness, in obedience to a summons issued by that District Judge intentionally omits to appear. A has committed the offence defined in this section

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 208 (Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 208 (Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant), Chapter XIII — Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) Whoever, being legally bound to attend in person or by an agent at a certain place and time in obedience to a summons, notice, order, or proclamation proceeding from any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to issue the same, intentionally omits to attend at that place or time or departs from the place where he is bound to attend before the time at which it is lawful for him to depart,–
   (2) (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both;
   (3) (b) where the summons, notice, order or proclamation is to attend in person or by agent in a Court with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 208 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 208 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

questionsAndAnswers.answer:
Introduction. BNS s. 208 deals with Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant. It sits in Chapter XIII — Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. After 1 July 2024 this is the current-law citation for this offence / definition / punishment.

Meaning. Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant. BNS restatement of IPC 174. Elements are substantially the same; cite the BNS number for offences on or after 1 July 2024. BNS restatement of IPC 174. Cite the BNS number for facts on or after 1 July 2024.

Legal rule. In student language: BNS s. 208 is the rule on “Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant”. The section provides that whoever, being legally bound to attend in person or by an agent at a certain place and time in obedience to a summons, notice, order, or proclamation proceeding from any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to issue the same, intentionally omits to attend at that place or time or departs from the place where he is bound to attend before the time at which it is lawful for him to depart,–. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Essential ingredients. An authoritative analysis must list them, not hide them in one paragraph:
1. Whoever, being legally bound to attend in person or by an agent at a certain place and time in obedience to a summons, notice, order, or proclamation proceeding from any public servant legally competent, as such public servant, to issue the same, intentionally omits to attend at that place or time or departs from the place where he is bound to attend before the time at which it is lawful for him to depart,–
2. (a) shall be punished with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to one month, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both;
3. (b) where the summons, notice, order or proclamation is to attend in person or by agent in a Court with simple imprisonment for a term which may extend to six months, or with fine which may extend to ten thousand rupees, or with both

Illustrations. The section itself supplies worked examples. In legal analysis, pick one illustration, restate its facts, and show which ingredient it proves. Illustration (a): (a) A, being legally bound to appear before a High Court, in obedience to a subpoena issuing from that Court, intentionally omits to appear. A has committed the offence defined in this section

Limitations. Apply only the conditions written in s. 208. Do not import a defence from a different chapter unless the question requires it.

Conclusion. BNS s. 208 is the complete current-law heading for Non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant. Define, list ingredients, use an illustration, note any explanation or exception, apply, cite. That is a complete statutory structure.

enhancement.detailedExplanation: Section 208 constitutes a key component of Chapter XIII (Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023, addressing non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant. The provision balances personal liberty with public interest and social order. The prosecution must establish every statutory element beyond reasonable doubt: the specified actus reus, the requisite mens rea, and any relevant statutory circumstances. Modern judicial interpretation emphasizes substantive fairness, proportionality in sentencing, and adherence to constitutional safeguards. Where statutory exceptions or provisos are attached to the section, the accused must establish facts bringing the case within such provisions under evidentiary standards.
examples: Teaching example (Standard application): An individual intentionally commits acts satisfying the statutory formula of non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant under Section 208 without lawful authority. The individual is liable under BNS s. 208.

Teaching example (Absence of mens rea / Lawful exception): A person acts in good faith or without the requisite statutory mental element under circumstances recognized by law. The essential ingredients of Section 208 are not satisfied; no penal liability attaches.
distinctions: Section 208 vs General Attempt: Section 208 penalizes the substantive conduct specified in Chapter XIII; inchoate attempts without specific provisions fall under the general attempt provisions.

Section 208 vs Cognate Chapter Offences: Liability under Section 208 is distinguished by its specific mental threshold and the particular legal interest protected under Of Contempts of the Lawful Authority of Public Servants.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether the accused is liable under BNS s. 208 for conduct relating to non-attendance in obedience to an order from public servant.
Rule: Under BNS s. 208, liability attaches upon proof of the statutory actus reus accompanied by the requisite mens rea without lawful justification.
Application: The evidence demonstrates that the accused performed the specified act with the required state of mind, satisfying all statutory ingredients of Section 208.
Conclusion: The accused is guilty of an offence under BNS s. 208 and subject to the prescribed punishment.
